b: My coworker, Rain, was hired into our crazy startup a few weeks back. They came with experience, including at startups, but the pace and chaos here appears to be throwing them regardless.

Rain is not the best at social cues. I have a soft spot in my heart for people like that and generally try to make space for them. But the stress of chaos plus obliviousness is manifesting as fussiness and distracting rabbit holes. I’m struggling to do as much as they apparently need me to do to keep them on track for our urgent deliverables and to stop them from annoying others (and me!).
Examples of things that are causing friction:

If I am invited to a meeting that Rain is not invited to, they ask me how they can be invited to that meeting too. I am not always in charge of who attends meetings, and I have already extended a lot of my own capital trying to get them included in things. The tone reads as fearful of being excluded. At the same time, when impromptu meetings happen nearby, Rain hangs back.

We are in crunch time, and we are all-hands-on-deck putting out fires. Rain asks to make fixed appointments to do things so that “they know what their day will look like.” I told them that’s fine with me as long as they understand the appointments may need to change on short notice, and I cautioned that I do not often know what my day will look like. When the appointments do change on short notice, they make mildly miffed comments about how they “didn’t think this would take so long” or how they planned to leave early to complete the workday from home and now will miss the activity. (The position was advertised as in-person, but we try to offer flexibility.)

When we run into a minor solvable hiccup with an activity (think an unexpected extra 30 minutes of work), they mention that they prefer to avoid such issues by performing all preparations the day before. This is after they have seen us running around all the time trying to put out fires and getting pulled into surprise meetings with the CEO. I deal with 30 minutes of unexpected work by reprioritizing or staying 30 minutes late.

We are trying to fix some hairy technical problems with extremely minimal time or resources. Rain has a tendency to have a reasonable but not revolutionary idea, then tell the team they have “solved” the issue without the background knowledge to know the depth of the problem or what has already been tried and before having done the work to prove the issue is indeed solved. This annoys the people who are working flat-out to contain the problem (and are catching the flak for it).

We perform hands-on, highly skilled, highly critical tasks that require attention and focus. In their first few days, I invited them to observe these tasks for their learning. They did not pick up that we needed to focus and continually asked questions and made comments during execution. After me repeatedly saying, “We can’t answer that right now because we need to focus” or “I am trying to focus right now,” Rain asked if I was asking them to stop talking. I said yes, laughed, and reiterated they were welcome to observe, but requested they write down questions for later and promised to schedule a debrief to make sure their questions got answered. They instead opted to not observe any tasks unless they could ask questions during it. They also mentioned that more mature companies do not allow new employees to observe critical tasks for this reason and maybe it was a learning opportunity for us that we should not have invited them to watch.

In Rain’s first two weeks, they had annoyed all immediate teammates. I was chosen as the envoy to have a stern conversation with them about picking their battles and trying to read the room more. I also tried to give them some backstory on what they were seeing and to validate that a lot of what we do is not best practice due to our company’s life stage and needs, but that it had worked for us so far. It seemed to help the behaviors some, but it was received with anxiety, fear of being targeted for criticism, and some defensive explanations of how really our processes are unreasonable to deal with (the rest of us deal) and that’s why they have been wrong-footed. It has not solved the issue.

My coworkers and I want Rain to be successful, which is a main reason we spoke to them first instead of to their manager. I am not confident the manager will not just decide they are a poor fit and cut losses. But I’m still having to deal with mildly miffed or confused comments when things are changing on the fly or are not being done by the book. We’re having to maneuver behind the scenes to make sure they do not anger any vendors or high-ranking people. Overall, they just are not appearing to get the memo.

But I feel guilty. When I first raised the issue, they expressed that they welcome direct communication and correction. Should I be snapping at them when they next comment about how I could have prevented my current challenges by better planning? Right now, I’m saying something polite but a little bit clipped like, “You’re not wrong that this could be better, but we had other priorities.” Or, when they are trying to make small talk at an inappropriate time, “I’m so sorry, but I really need to focus on this work right now.” I was raised southern — I’m struggling to be more blunt in the moment! Do I need to schedule more dedicated sit-down conversations?
I am not Rain’s supervisor, but I am influential with leadership and may be asked for feedback on them if it comes to a head. What do you recommend I do if this behavior continues?
Realistically, it sounds like Rain may not be suited for this job and this culture.

That happens! Not everyone is suited to every work environment. You don’t need to keep bending over backwards to try to force them to work out if it’s just a mismatch … and you definitely shouldn’t be spending your own capital on things like getting them invited to meetings that don’t make sense for them to be in, or maneuvering so they don’t anger vendors or VIPs. You sound like you’ve taken on the burden of making this work out, but you’re just a peer; you don’t have that ability (and you wouldn’t necessarily have that ability even if you were Rain’s manager). Rain’s boss really needs to be looped in about what’s going on.

However, if you want to try one final conversation — particularly since Rain has said they welcome direct communication — the kindest thing would be to lay out, essentially, “I know you prefer to work like X, but the reality of this job is Y and you’ll need to decide if that works for you or not.” (For what it’s worth, though, “I welcome direct communication” does not always turn out to mean the person really does welcome direct communication in practice…)

Here’s a sample script: “I’ve noticed you seem frustrated with some things about the job, and you mentioned you prefer direct communication so I thought it might be useful for me to lay out what I’m seeing. My sense from working together is that there’s a mismatch between how you prefer to work and what this particular environment requires. I can see that you value clear structure, advance planning, and being able to understand things thoroughly before you move forward, and those are all reasonable things to want. The reality here, though, is that we’re operating with limited resources, and priorities shift a lot. We often have to make decisions with incomplete information, interrupt plans to deal with something more urgent, and do some things in a less-than-ideal way because it’s what the situation requires. That isn’t everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s the reality of our jobs here, and I want to be candid with you about it so you can decide if you’re comfortable with the idea of working that way or not.”

You could also say something like, “I also wanted to see if I can help you calibrate when to raise concerns. Having ideas, asking questions, and identifying problems are all valuable, but the timing will really affect how it’s received. If we’re in the middle of a critical task, we need to focus. If we’re putting out a fire, we need to prioritize solving it before we discuss how we could have prevented it. There’s a time for those discussions, but not when it will distract from work that needs to happen right now.”

This doesn’t cover all the problems — it doesn’t address Rain’s tendency to declare problems solved without knowing what they’re talking about, for example — but it gets at some of the biggest. In theory, if you did want to include that too, you could say something like, “When we’re working on a complicated technical problem, you sometimes declare an issue solved before you’ve fully understood it and what’s already been tried, and that can be frustrating for the people actively troubleshooting it. It’ll go over better if you take the time to understand what’s already been tried, consult the people closest to the problem, and make sure that any solution actually works.” But frankly, I think that’s too much and at that point Rain is likely to feel they can’t do anything right. So I’d focus just on the previous two paragraphs instead, and if they do solve those, you can raise this piece of it later.
But ultimately, this is a pretty significant mismatch, it’s not your job to solve, and it may not be solvable.
